steps.label: 3.1: Models and Simulators
steps.content:
Data Models and Collection

3.1: Models and Simulators

Year 8

  • Today: what a model is, and its parts.
  • The big question: why does a model need good data?
Think → Pair → ShareHow does a weather forecast know about tomorrow before it happens?Show the answer

A computer works it out from data about today. Today we see how.

steps.label: What Is a Model?
steps.content:
What Is a Model?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: why would a company test a new car on a computer before it builds one?Show the worked answer

Building a real car to test is slow and costs a lot. A computer version can be tried first.

Why? The computer version acts like the real car, so it shows problems early.

A model is a simple computer version of a real system. It works things out, so it can predict what will happen.

  • A weather forecast predicts tomorrow's rain.
  • A traffic model shows how long the queue gets.
  • A rabbit model predicts how many rabbits there will be.
  • A simulator is a model you use like the real thing.
  • A flight simulator: a pilot flies, and the screen acts like a real plane.
  • A model is simpler than the real system.

steps.label: The Parts of a Model
steps.content:
The Parts of a Model

Think → Pair → SharePredict: how many rabbits after 3 years? Why do we need the rule to work it out?Show the worked answer

20, then 40, then 80, then 160.

Why? The input alone is only the start. The rule says how it changes each year.

A rabbit model.

Inputs (data)
20 rabbits at the start
→
Rules
Each year, the number of rabbits doubles.
→
Outputs
Rabbits after 3 years
  • Inputs: the data that goes in.
  • Rules: the calculations that work out the answer.
  • Outputs: the predictions that come out.
  • Simplified: it leaves out things like foxes and weather.

steps.content:
Why Use a Model?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: a new pilot must practise an engine failure. Why not practise in a real plane?Show the worked answer

A mistake in a real plane could kill people and wreck the plane.

Why? In a simulator, a crash hurts no one and costs nothing. The pilot can try again.

steps.label: Why the Data Matters
steps.content:
Why the Data Matters

Think → Pair → ShareSomeone types 200 instead of 20. Predict the output. Why is the rule not to blame?Show the worked answer

200, 400, 800, 1600 rabbits. The real island has about 160.

Why? The rule is right. The input was wrong, so the output is wrong too.

The data makes a model match the real system.

Inputs (data)
20 rabbits (counted)
→
Rules
Doubles each year
→
Outputs
160 after 3 years
  • Wrong data in gives a wrong prediction out.
  • We call this garbage in, garbage out.
  • Good data is correct, up to date and complete.

steps.label: Compare: Good Data, Missing Data
steps.content:
Compare: Good Data, Missing Data

Think → Pair → ShareBoth use the same rule. Predict each output. Why does only one match the real account?Show the worked answer

A: 100 + 4 x 10 = 140. B: 0 + 4 x 10 = 40.

Why? B is missing the start amount, so it begins at 0. The rule cannot fix missing data.

A savings model. Rule: each week, add 10. Real account after 4 weeks: 140.
